prompt.context: African Gold Mines Co. (AGM) is a junior gold producer with one open-pit mine currently in production in Cameroon. The mine was established 10 years ago, and forecasts predict at least another 10 years of consistent gold production. Last year, AGM produced 250,000 oz of gold from their mine. They have come to us as their profit level has been slowly decreasing over the past five years. They had numerous operational issues with the mining equipment, problems with the workers' union, and issues with community relations notably.
prompt.question: They want us to investigate what is the best course of action for their operation to return to their previous level of profitability within 12 to 24 months. They want us to specifically focus our attention on the mining department of the company.

clarifying_info.q: Have costs or revenues changed over the past five years?
clarifying_info.a: Costs have increased by 20% over the past 5 years. Revenues for the entire company in 2019 were $375m.

clarifying_info.q: What were the mining department costs in the most recent year?
What is the specific profitability target?
clarifying_info.a: The target is to return to profitability level of 5 years ago, meaning reducing costs by $6m. (Cost 5 years ago = $36m / 1.2 = $30m; cost reduction needed = $36m - $30m = $6m.)

exhibits.title: Revenue Structure of AGM
exhibits.shows: A dual-axis chart covering 2013–2019 showing AGM's annual gold production (in tonnes/oz, left axis) as bars and the average annual gold price ($ per ounce, right axis) as a line.
exhibits.data: Gold production ranges across years with the 2019 figure at approximately 250,000 oz; gold price ranges roughly $1,000–$1,550 per ounce over 2013–2019; total revenues have remained approximately flat across the period.

exhibits.title: Cost Structure of AGM Mining Department
exhibits.shows: Two charts: (1) a pie chart of the cost composition of mining operations — Equipment Maintenance 30%, Fuel 27%, Salary 28%, Overhead 10%, Other 5%; (2) a table of year-on-year cost variation by category from 2015 to 2019, alongside a line chart of average annual Brent Crude oil price.

exhibits.title: Truck Selection Alternatives for AGM
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of four truck fleet alternatives plus the current situation, showing CAPEX, annual maintenance cost, fuel consumption (L/hr), and expected fleet life for each option.
exhibits.data: Current Caterpillar 777E: CAPEX $0.1m, maintenance $540k/yr, 95 L/hr, 1 yr life; Overhaul 777E: CAPEX $0.6m, maintenance $500k/yr, 80 L/hr, 5 yr life; New Caterpillar 777E: CAPEX $1.0m, maintenance $340k/yr, 60 L/hr, 10 yr life; Komatsu HD785-7: CAPEX $1.2m, maintenance $450k/yr, 70 L/hr, 12 yr life; Caterpillar 780D Autonomous Semi-Electric: CAPEX $1.6m, maintenance $360k/yr, 40 L/hr, 8 yr life.

framework: Revenue branch: Price (market-driven, limited control) × Volume (geology-driven, limited control) → revenues are stable and not actionable
Cost branch: Focus on mining department — break down by cost category (maintenance, fuel, salary, overhead, other)
Identify cost categories with the highest share and fastest-growing trend
Prioritize investigation of equipment maintenance and fuel consumption as the largest and fastest-rising costs
Evaluate fleet replacement alternatives on a total-cost-per-year basis
Recommend the option that meets the $6m cost-reduction target and consider qualitative/strategic criteria

questions.prompt: After reviewing Exhibit 1, what can you conclude about revenues, and where should the investigation focus?
questions.guidance: Strong answer: Revenue is roughly flat despite year-to-year fluctuations in both gold price and production. Gold prices are commodity-market-driven — AGM cannot influence them. Production volumes are geology-limited and set by the long-term mine plan. Therefore, revenues are not actionable in the short term. The investigation must shift entirely to the cost side.

questions.prompt: What do you think are the biggest cost drivers in a mining operation? Which should we focus on and why?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm a structured list of mining cost categories (variable vs. fixed, or by item). Key categories: equipment maintenance, fuel, labor/salary, overhead, consumables/explosives, environmental/regulatory. Candidate should prioritize by size and controllability — maintenance and fuel are large and appear controllable via fleet decisions, while salary is large but operationally sensitive (union issues). Candidate should articulate why s/he ranks the focus areas.

questions.prompt: Based on Exhibit 2, which cost categories are driving the profitability decline, and what action should follow?
questions.guidance: Equipment maintenance (30% of cost base, +3%/+9%/+9%/+12%/+19% YoY over 5 years) and fuel (27% of cost base, +3%/+3%/+5%/+9%/+13% YoY) are clearly the two main drivers — both share is large and trend is accelerating. Salary is large (28%) but growth is near-zero. The Brent oil price chart contextualizes part of the fuel increase. Candidate should connect rising oil prices to fuel costs and deteriorating equipment to maintenance escalation. Next step: investigate fleet replacement options.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3 and the additional information provided, calculate the total annual cost per truck for each alternative and identify the best financial option(s).
questions.guidance: Candidate should annualize CAPEX via straight-line depreciation (CAPEX / expected life), then add annual maintenance and fuel cost. Fuel cost = fuel consumption (L/hr) × operating hours/yr × fuel price. Operating hours = 20 hrs/day × 300 days = 6,000 hr/yr. Fuel price = $1/L. Fleet = 20 trucks. Both New Caterpillar 777E and Caterpillar 780D tie at $800k/truck/yr — the lowest total cost. Both meet the $6m savings requirement: savings = ($1,210k - $800k) × 20 trucks = $8.2m/yr, which exceeds the $6m target.

math.setup: For each alternative: Total cost/truck/yr = (CAPEX / life) + maintenance/yr + (fuel L/hr × 6,000 hr/yr × $1/L). Fleet savings vs. current = (current total cost/truck - alternative total cost/truck) × 20 trucks.
steps: Operating hours per truck per year: 20 hr/day × 300 days = 6,000 hr/yr
Current 777E: fuel = 95 × 6,000 × $1 = $570k; maintenance = $540k; CAPEX ann. = $100k/1 = $100k; total = $1,210k/truck/yr
Overhaul 777E: fuel = 80 × 6,000 = $480k; maintenance = $500k; CAPEX ann. = $600k/5 = $120k; total = $1,100k/truck/yr
New 777E: fuel = 60 × 6,000 = $360k; maintenance = $340k; CAPEX ann. = $1,000k/10 = $100k; total = $800k/truck/yr
Komatsu HD785-7: fuel = 70 × 6,000 = $420k; maintenance = $450k; CAPEX ann. = $1,200k/12 = $100k; total = $970k/truck/yr
Caterpillar 780D Autonomous: fuel = 40 × 6,000 = $240k; maintenance = $360k; CAPEX ann. = $1,600k/8 = $200k; total = $800k/truck/yr
math.answer: New Caterpillar 777E and Caterpillar 780D Autonomous are tied at $800k/truck/yr (total fleet cost ~$16m/yr). Annual fleet savings = $8.2m vs. current situation, exceeding the $6m target. Both options are financially equivalent.

questions.prompt: Since the two best options are financially tied, what qualitative criteria and risks should AGM consider when choosing between the New 777E and the 780D Autonomous?
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure a pros/cons or risk framework for both options. Key dimensions: technology readiness and remote-site support, supply chain and spare parts, workforce/labor implications (union context, community relations), safety, environmental (GHG), training requirements, operational efficiency, and option for further cost reduction if fuel prices rise. See brainstorming section for detailed sample.

brainstorming.prompt: What criteria and risks should AGM consider when choosing between the New Caterpillar 777E and the Caterpillar 780D Autonomous Semi-Electric truck?

categories.name: New Caterpillar 777E — Pros
ideas: Same model already in use — same spare parts and supply chain
Same maintenance processes already known to AGM
Workforce already trained; no retraining cost
10-year fleet life (longer than 780D's 8 years)
Proven technology in remote African settings

categories.name: New Caterpillar 777E — Cons
ideas: Higher fuel consumption than 780D — more exposed to future oil price increases
Requires continuous operator training
Potentially lower operational efficiency vs. autonomous
Higher GHG emissions vs. semi-electric option

categories.name: Caterpillar 780D Autonomous — Pros
ideas: Lowest fuel consumption (40 L/hr) — greater upside if oil prices rise
Potential for further cost savings by reducing driver headcount
Improved safety (no driver in hazardous pit area)
Potential for increased operational efficiency (24/7 autonomous cycle)
No operator training required
Lower GHG emissions — better ESG profile

categories.name: Caterpillar 780D Autonomous — Cons
ideas: New technology — may be harder to implement and maintain at a remote site in Cameroon
Technical support and spare parts supply chain may be difficult to establish remotely
Maintenance and IT/operations personnel will require specialized training hard to source locally
Old parts inventory for 777E may become unusable
Laying off truck drivers in a small village community could damage community relations (already an AGM issue)
Shorter fleet life: 8 years vs. 10 years for new 777E
Higher CAPEX ($1.6m vs. $1.0m per truck)

recommendation: AGM has a cost problem driven primarily by rapidly escalating equipment maintenance costs (up ~19% YoY in 2019) and fuel costs (up ~13% YoY), which together account for 57% of the mining department's $36m cost base.

To restore profitability to the level of 5 years ago (reducing costs by $6m), AGM should replace its entire fleet of 20 mining trucks. Both the New Caterpillar 777E and the Caterpillar 780D Autonomous are financially equivalent at $800k/truck/yr, generating $8.2m in annual fleet savings — exceeding the $6m target.

(Candidate should choose one and defend it.) If recommending New 777E: lower implementation risk, proven technology in the remote Cameroon context, same supply chain, workforce continuity — critical given existing union and community-relations tensions. If recommending 780D Autonomous: lowest fuel exposure, safety upside, ESG benefit, and long-run labor cost reduction potential if workforce issues can be managed sensitively.
risks: 777E: Continued exposure to oil price increases; no step-change in operational efficiency.
780D: Technology implementation risk in a remote site; community backlash if drivers are laid off; specialized maintenance talent scarce locally; new supply chain to establish.
Both: Savings projections assume fuel price of $1/L — actual savings will vary with oil markets.
Labor/union: Any workforce changes must be managed carefully given pre-existing union tensions.
next_steps: Conduct a detailed on-site feasibility assessment for autonomous truck deployment in Cameroon (connectivity, terrain, regulatory environment).
Engage the workers' union and community early regarding any workforce transition plan.
Issue RFPs / negotiate pricing for preferred fleet option to confirm CAPEX assumptions.
Model sensitivity of savings to fuel price scenarios ($0.80–$1.50/L) to stress-test the recommendation.
Define implementation timeline and milestones to hit the 12–24-month profitability target.
